{{Dynamic list}}

Math ability is passed from parent to child<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2016/09/160901125401.htm|title=Parents' math skills 'rub off' on their children|access-date=2025-04-09}}</ref> with the most famous example being the [[Bernoulli family]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://galileo-unbound.blog/2020/10/06/the-bountiful-bernoulli-of-basel/|title=The Bountiful Bernoullis of Basel|date=6 October 2020 |access-date=2025-04-09}}</ref> This [[List of second-generation physicists|second generation phenomenon also holds in physics]]<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.wondersofphysics.com/2022/06/father-son-nobel-prize.html#google_vignette|title=4 Father-Son Nobel Prize Winners In Physics|access-date=2025-04-09}}</ref> but in that field the [[Nobel Prize in Physics]] gives a tool for tracking it, since it has been given out for more than 120 years, and there are on average more than two Nobel Prizes in Physics given each year.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://baryon.be/stories/nobelprize/#:~:text=In%20recent%20years%2C%20the%20Nobel,War%2C%20it%20was%20only%201.2./|title=The Nobel Prize in Physics|access-date=2025-04-09}}</ref> There is no comparable award in mathematics<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.snopes.com/fact-check/the-prizes-rite/|title=No Nobel Prize for Math|date=2 March 2001 |access-date=2025-04-09}}</ref> but perusing (for example) the [[MacTutor History of Mathematics Archive]]<ref>{{cite web|url=https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/|title=MacTutor|access-date=2025-04-09}}</ref> list of biographies enables the construction of a similar list of notable two-generation pairs of mathematicians.

The following is a list of parent-child pairs who both made contributions to mathematics significant enough to be noted in the citation for a prestigious prize, in an obituary in a major math journal, or in a similarly authoritative source. All are father-son except for [[Emmy Noether]] and [[Cathleen Morawetz]].  The list is in chronological order by birth date of the parent.
